newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST-Telkom cash boosts S.African May reserves.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Telkom cash boosts S.African May reserves.

text.p: Foreign exchange inflows from the part privatisation of state telecommunications concern Telkom will boost May official reserves by over 20 percent, according to 10 economists polled by Reuters.
The consensus forecast is for central bank reserves of gold and foreign exchange reserves to surge to 17.70 billion rand in May from April's 14.40 billion.
The headline reserves figure for the month will be released at 1600 GMT on Monday.
That would be an all-time high in rand terms. But in dollars it equates to less than $4.0 billion against nearly $4.3 billion in December 1995, before the rand started its tumble.
It also still represents less than two months import cover.

"We should see a very good figure due to the Telkom money but the number could be affected if the Reserve Bank makes any repayment of short term credits," said Henry Flint, economist at Mathison and Hollidge.

A U.S.-Malaysian consortium paid $1.26 billion rand for a 30 percent stake in Telkom of which around $1 billion went to Telkom itself to fund future investment and was mopped up earlier this month by the central Reserve Bank.
Analysts said it was unclear how much of this cash would show up on the Bank's balance sheet at the month-end but most expected a major contribution from the deal.
In addition, reserves would be swelled by net foreign purchases of shares and bonds over the month of around three billion rand.

On the downside, there would have been a major outflow following Illovo Sugar Ltd's purchase of 94.25 percent of Lonrho Sugar for 1.62 billion rand. In addition, some economists said the central bank probably spent some forex to stop the rand going through 4.50 on the dollar earlier this month.

The big imponderable in the number is whether or not the Reserve Bank will use May's inflows to repay some or all of the 2.5 billion rand in short-term credits taken out earlier this year. That resulted in a wide variance of forecasts from eonomists, ranging from 16 billion rand to 20 billion.

The majority opinion, however, was that the Reserve Bank would opt to retain its recent borrowings as a buffer against any major outflows following the relaxation of exchange controls on individuals which takes effect from July 1.
"I don't think they will repay any of the credits. I think they will hold on to as much as possible in case of any potential outflows after July 1," said Dawie Roodt of Equisec.
